previous.passage: Port of Spain was still dark when my mother, Pearl, drove me to the diner on the highway for one last breakfast before my flight. I am Cecile, her only child, and I was leaving for a college in Toronto. She slid a wrapped box across the table: a wool scarf in the colors of a school I had not chosen, the one she had hoped for. I thanked her and put it on at once, over a T-shirt, in the heat. She praised how it looked. We ate saltfish and bake and talked about the weather in Canada. Only on the plane did I notice that she had sewn my initials into the fringe, crooked, by hand, the work of several nights. I wore it through every winter that followed, and I never told her that I knew she knew.

previous.passage: Four stones mark the safe path across the dry riverbed below our town in Oaxaca, and Nicolas taught me to count them aloud before I was old enough to ask why. Every crossing, my stepfather named them: the flat one, the split one, the one shaped like a shoe, the last. The summer my scholarship letter came, he walked me to the bus on the far bank. I, Katarzyna, the girl who had never left the valley, talked the whole way about tuition, about the cost of the ticket north, about how he would manage the stall alone. He answered none of it. __At the third stone he stopped, tapped it twice with his boot, and waited until I said its name.__ On the far bank he set down my suitcase and told me the river would be running by the time I came home, and that I should not try to cross it by memory.

previous.passage: When the band paused between songs, Tommaso came in through the kitchen door of the wedding hall as if he had stepped out for ice twenty minutes earlier instead of nine years. Aaliyah, the bride, did not know him; she saw only that her new mother-in-law set down her fork and did not pick it up again. He wore a pressed suit a size too large and carried a gift wrapped in newspaper. No one asked where he had been, and he offered nothing, only kissed his mother's cheek and took the empty chair by the cake table that someone, it seemed, had been keeping. Gossip along the Delta levees had long since called him a scoundrel. Yet the cake was cut beneath his hand, and the old woman ate two pieces, and the bride, watching, decided that some absences are settled in ways a guest list cannot show.

previous.passage: I was twelve when Mohan came home from the border and took over our grandfather's clock shop in Kochi, and I assumed he did it because no one else would. He was clumsy at first; his hands, which had cleaned rifles for six years, shook over the hairsprings. Still, every evening he cleared a space on the bench and set a loupe in front of me. I complained. Tourists bought quartz watches from the stalls; nobody, I told him, would pay to fix a pendulum. He agreed, and kept handing me the tweezers. I learned to hear the beat of an escapement before I learned to like him again. Now, when customers ask Sunja who taught her, I say my brother, and I let them assume he was a master. He was not. He was a man who practiced late at night so he could stay one lesson ahead of me.

previous.passage: Callum stepped off my father's boat in the summer of 1912 with a botanist's case and a cough, and asked within the hour why our tea bushes grew only on the western slope above the Galway shore. I was fourteen and found the question rude. Every child on the estate knew the east field was poor ground; my father, Lachlan, said so at supper each night, the way other men said grace. Callum walked the east rows anyway, crumbled the soil between his fingers, and said the trouble was the drainage ditch my grandfather had dug, not the earth. My father thanked him and refilled his cup. The ditch stayed. Callum left on the September ferry, and I rowed him across myself, cross that he had been right and that we would go on as if he had not. I still keep the soil sample he left on our windowsill, labeled in his small hand.

previous.passage: Taipei's hills were not supposed to hold vineyards, Mingyu told me, which was why he had planted one. We were strangers waiting out a washed-out road on his porch, my rented scooter tipped in the mud, rows of purple grapes dripping behind us. When I said my name was Xinyi, he repeated it twice, as if testing its weight. I asked how he had started. He said a teacher, forty years ago, had read his essay about his father's tea farm aloud and remarked, not unkindly, that it was a good essay about the wrong crop. He laughed telling it. Then he handed me shears and showed me how to cut a bunch without bruising its neighbors. By the time the road crew arrived, my hands were sticky and I had filled two baskets. I never learned what the teacher meant, and I doubt Mingyu had ever settled it.
